title: The Well of Old Chapel Road
premise: Ansel Dravenmoor hosts the graveyard-shift call-in show 'Nightline' from a studio in a decommissioned chapel on Old Chapel Road, where her regular callers are all people who died the previous week—she keeps the ritual of counting doors and burning lights because the ritual is what keeps the dead polite. When an excavation crew breaches a door sealed from the inside beneath the chapel, the calls stop being confessions and start being instructions, and Ansel learns the show was inherited: every host before her signed a contract with whatever was invited in during the chapel's congregant days, trading their memory of being loved for the power to speak with the dead. As the last resident of the house above the dig site moves to sign the papers that would transfer the entity's lease to the town itself, Ansel must survive one night of the door being open, reconstruct the erased memory of her own mother's signing, and choose between burning the well that feeds the show or becoming its next voice. She burns it—losing every caller, every dead voice, and her mother's face from memory—and signs nothing, walking out at sunrise into a silence that is finally, mercifully empty.
about_author: Juniper Lockridge is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent six years working the dead hours of small-market AM and swears half her callers sounded pre-recorded. She writes horror about small towns that keep their promises, and she still counts the doors when she enters a building.

chapters.title: The Dead Air Hours
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. We meet the ritual: lights on, doors counted, calls taken from listeners who died last week. A woman named Cora calls to apologize for something she never said in life. The beat is eerie competence—Ansel is good at this, and the reader should feel both comfort and wrongness in that.

chapters.title: Old Chapel Road
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, with flashback texture. History of the chapel-turned-studio: deconsecrated in 1961, sold cheap, always cheap, always to someone alone. Ansel inherited the lease from a host she never met, along with a binder of rules. Emotional beat: the loneliness of being chosen by a building.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Crews begin digging behind the chapel for a storm drain; Ansel feels the show's signal degrade as the machines bite deeper. That night, Cora's call cuts to static and a second voice breathes her name. Beat: the ritual is not protection, it's containment—and something is loosening.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: Ansel and the crew foreman, Denny, POV alternating. The crew unearths a door—oak, iron-banded, hinges on the inside, no handle outside. Denny jokes; Ansel doesn't. That night the door count comes up thirteen in a building with twelve. Beat: dread arriving as arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Binder of Rules
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. She rereads her predecessor's binder and finds pages torn out, edges burned. A rule she'd never needed is underlined twice: never let them finish a sentence that starts with 'remember when.' That night, a caller starts the sentence. Beat: the past was edited, and the editor wanted something forgotten.

chapters.title: Cora, Last Week
chapters.summary: Cora's POV, alive and then dead. A tender chapter: Cora's ordinary life, her death, her first call. Through her we see what the show gives the dead—one hour of being heard—and what it costs them. Beat: grief made functional; the show is a kindness with a mechanism inside it.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. She learns the house above the dig site has a sole occupant, Elias Vann, who is finalizing paperwork to deed the whole parcel—including the chapel and whatever is beneath it—to the town. A lawyer visits Ansel with papers of her own she never signed. Beat: the horror is bureaucratic; inheritance is a paper trail.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Denny's POV. Denny's crew finds a congregation ledger in the spoil heap: 1959, a revival, a door built and sealed after 'the visitor stayed past the amen.' Denny starts hearing the show on radios with no batteries. Beat: curiosity curdling into complicity—he wants to open the door.

chapters.title: The Voice That Signs
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The second voice on the line identifies itself as 'the resident' and speaks in Ansel's mother's cadence. It offers her a deal: sign the transfer yourself, keep the show, keep the dead. It knows things only her mother knew. Beat: temptation wearing a beloved voice.

chapters.title: Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, a long night in the studio. The lights fail one by one as the door below works upward through the building's architecture; each burned-out bulb is a door she can no longer count. Cora calls to warn her, breaking the rules to do it. Beat: the ritual failing, and a dead woman breaking protocol out of love.

chapters.title: The Torn Pages
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. She tracks down the estate of her predecessor, Ruth Okafor, and finds the burned fragments: every host before her signed, and every host's memory of being loved was taken as payment. Ruth's last note: 'The well is under the chapel. The show is the pump. Do not drink.' Beat: inheritance revealed as predation.

chapters.title: Elias Vann's House
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias is dying and wants the land gone from the family; his grandfather built the door. He shows Ansel the original invitation—a written covenant, signed by nine congregants, that renews with every deed transfer. The town's purchase would make the whole town the signatory. Beat: the scale of the trap becomes civic.

chapters.title: Static Sermon
chapters.summary: The entity's POV, briefly and horribly, then Ansel's. During broadcast, the entity preaches through Ansel's own mouth for ninety seconds; callers weep with recognition. She wakes with an hour missing and a signature half-formed in her notebook. Beat: the body as territory; power beginning to corrupt her from the inside.

chapters.title: What My Mother Signed
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, the emotional center. She reconstructs the erased memory: her mother was Ruth Okafor's engineer, and she signed to bring Ansel back from a childhood fever—the show's first miracle, its first corruption of love. Ansel's grief and fury arrive together. Beat: inheritance as wound.

chapters.title: The Town Meeting
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Ansel interrupts the council vote on the Vann parcel and tells the truth; the room hears her as a madwoman until the PA system in the empty building answers her, unprompted, in nine voices. The vote stalls. Beat: public disbelief cracking against one undeniable wrongness.

chapters.title: Denny Opens the Door
chapters.summary: Denny's POV. Compelled by the voice he's been hearing—his dead brother's—Denny breaks the seal at 11:40 p.m. The well exhales. The chapter ends with the door standing open on darkness that is not empty, and Denny stepping aside to let it climb. Beat: catastrophe by kindness; the door was never locked, only shut.

chapters.title: Thirteen
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, the siege begins. Every dead caller arrives at once, not as threats but as witnesses, crowding the studio as the entity walks the building, opening doors she has already counted. The lights hold only where Cora stands. Beat: terror braided with loyalty—the dead choose sides.

chapters.title: The Covenant
chapters.summary: Ansel and Elias's POV. They reach the well chamber with the original covenant; the entity offers its final terms: sign, and the dead stay, the show continues, her mother's voice endures forever. Ansel reads the fine print aloud—'in perpetuity, in all voices'—and understands the town would become a mouth. Beat: the temptation at its most reasonable.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The covenant can be voided before dawn only by a signatory's blood and a host's refusal—her mother's signature, her own refusal. She calls the show one last time and asks the dead, all of them, whether they want to stay. The line is silent, then Cora: 'Let us go.' Beat: consent, freely given, as the only clean power in the book.

chapters.title: The Well of Old Chapel Road
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, the climax. She cuts her palm over the covenant, speaks her refusal into every open microphone, and drops the pages into the well. The building screams through nine throats; the door slams itself; the lights surge and die. She holds the broadcast open through the last dark hour, alone, saying nothing, letting the dead air be dead. Beat: sacrifice as broadcast—her final show is silence.

chapters.title: Sign the Papers
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At sunrise she refuses the town's transfer papers in front of the lawyer and the council; Elias tears up his deed. The excavation is filled. She remembers her mother's face only as a fact now, not a feeling, and grieves the payment she can't get back. Beat: victory with a permanent cost—the theme of inheritance paid in full.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, epilogue. Months later, she hosts a normal show for the living—insomniacs, truckers, the lonely—and takes no calls from the dead, because there are none. On her last night at the chapel before the demolition, she counts the doors one final time: twelve. Beat: peace as emptiness; the ritual kept out of love, not fear, and then released.
